content: Approximately 350 million individuals worldwide are chronic carriers of the hepatitis B virus (HBV), placing them at an elevated risk of developing severe complications such as liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. For over 2,000 years, Chinese medicinal herbs have been extensively utilized in the treatment of chronic liver diseases. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Chinese medicinal herbs in treating asymptomatic carriers of HBV. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Trials Register, The Cochrane Library, The Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and hand-searched Chinese journals and conference proceedings, as of October 2000. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized trials with a minimum follow-up period of three months. These trials compared Chinese medicinal herbs (either as single herbs or herbal compounds) against placebo, no intervention, general non-specific treatments, or interferon therapy. Studies that compared the combination of Chinese medicinal herbs and interferon with interferon alone were also included. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, and analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis whenever feasible. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were stratified by factors such as ethnic origin, age at the time of infection, and whether a single herb or a compound of herbs was used. The review included three randomized clinical trials involving a total of 307 patients, all of whom were followed for at least three months after the conclusion of treatment. The methodological quality of these trials was deemed poor. Among the herbal compounds studied, the Jianpi Wenshen recipe demonstrated significant effects on viral markers when compared to interferon therapy. Specifically, the relative risk (RR) for clearance of serum HBsAg was 2.40 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01 to 5.72), for clearance of HBeAg was 2.03 (95% CI 0.98 to 4.20), and for seroconversion of HBeAg to anti-HBe was 2.54 (95% CI 1.13 to 5.70). However, other herbs such as Phyllanthus amarus and Astragalus membranaceus did not exhibit significant antiviral effects when compared to placebo. An analysis pooling data from eight randomized clinical trials with follow-up periods of less than three months did not reveal any significant benefits of Chinese medicinal herbs on viral markers. Furthermore, there was a lack of data regarding long-term clinical outcomes and quality of life for the patients. In conclusion, based on evidence from a single low-quality trial, the herbal compound Jianpi Wenshen recipe may possess antiviral activity in asymptomatic carriers of HBV. However, the current evidence is insufficient to recommend the use of Chinese medicinal herbs for this condition. High-quality, rigorously designed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials are necessary to establish their efficacy and safety.
